title: DOJ Withheld 53 Pages of Epstein Files Naming Trump Including FBI 302s
description_short: DOJ Withheld 53 Pages of Epstein Files Naming Trump Including FBI 302s
description_medium: The DOJ withheld 53 pages of Epstein files mentioning Trump from initial releases, including three FBI FD-302 interview summaries from 2019 regarding an allegation that Trump sexually assaulted a 13-to-15-year-old circa 1983. Released March 5, 2026 after an NPR investigation revealed missing documents. As of March 2026, 37 pages remained missing. Deputy AG Todd Blanche stated We did not protect President Trump in the releases but was criticized for delaying release.
description_long: The supplied account describes 53 pages of Epstein-related material mentioning Trump that were absent from initial Justice Department releases. Among the documents were three FBI FD-302 interview summaries from 2019 involving a survivor's allegation that Trump sexually assaulted her when she was between 13 and 15, around 1983. Material was released on March 5, 2026 after NPR reporting identified the omissions, while 37 pages remained missing as of that month. The existence of interview records documents an allegation, not proof that the alleged assault occurred. The disclosure issue is also distinct from the allegation's truth: the record concerns what was withheld, subsequently released and still absent. Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche said the department had not protected Trump in the releases, a denial that should remain attributed alongside criticism of the delay. The supplied material does not establish a final legal determination about the alleged conduct or explain every remaining omission.

title: $TRUMP falls roughly 50% after Melania Trump launches $MELANIA memecoin
description_short: $TRUMP falls roughly 50% after Melania Trump launches $MELANIA memecoin
description_medium: Melania Trump announced the $MELANIA memecoin on January 19, 2025, one day after Donald Trump's $TRUMP token debuted. $TRUMP fell about 48% in the immediate reaction; the Guardian reported that roughly $7.5 billion of its market capitalization was erased within about ten minutes. Contemporary reports put $MELANIA's peak or fully diluted valuation in a wide range depending on metric and time, so the stored $30 billion loss claim should be removed.
description_long: Melania Trump announced the $MELANIA memecoin on January 19, 2025, a day after Donald Trump's $TRUMP token debuted. Contemporary reporting described an immediate fall of about 48% in $TRUMP, with roughly $7.5 billion of market capitalization erased in about ten minutes. The sequence documents a sharp market reaction to a second Trump-family token launch. Market capitalization is a valuation measure, however, and is not equivalent to a verified sum of losses realized by individual investors. Reports also used different measures and moments when describing $MELANIA's peak or fully diluted valuation. Those differences make it important to label the figure being used rather than combine estimates into a larger unsupported loss total. The supplied correction rejects the previous $30 billion assertion. The supported explanation records the launch dates and the reported immediate $TRUMP movement, while leaving the eventual performance of either token and investor-specific outcomes outside this event's established facts.

title: Moodys Chief Economist Confirms Tariffs Have Done Significant Damage to US Economy
description_short: Moodys Chief Economist Confirms Tariffs Have Done Significant Damage to US Economy
description_medium: On May 6, 2026 Moodys Analytics chief economist Mark Zandi published a note stating the data are definitive that Trumps tariffs have done significant damage to the economy. A Congressional Democratic study released the same month found American households will pay an average of 2512 dollars in tariff costs in 2026, up 44 percent from 1745 in 2025, while consumers already face elevated costs from the U.S.-Iran war driving up energy prices.
description_long: Moody's Analytics chief economist Mark Zandi wrote on May 6, 2026 that the data showed significant economic damage from Trump's tariffs. His assessment should remain attributed to him rather than presented as a formal judgment by a court or a consensus estimate from every economist. A separate congressional Democratic study released that month estimated average household tariff costs of $2,512 in 2026, up 44% from $1,745 in 2025. These figures are estimates from the study, not a verified bill received by every household. The supplied account also identifies higher energy costs associated with the U.S.–Iran war as part of the consumer-price context. That makes it important not to attribute all household cost increases to tariffs alone. The supported event combines a named economist's assessment with a separately attributed congressional estimate. It does not establish identical effects across income groups, a final annual outcome, or a single cause for every price change.

title: Nursing Home Tax Fraudster Pardoned After 960000 in Lobbying Fees to Trump-Linked Operatives
description_short: Nursing Home Tax Fraudster Pardoned After 960000 in Lobbying Fees to Trump-Linked Operatives
description_medium: Joseph Schwartz, a nursing home operator who pleaded guilty to a 38 million dollar payroll tax fraud scheme, was pardoned by Trump in November 2025 after serving just three months of a three-year sentence. Schwartz paid 960000 dollars to Trump-linked lobbyists Jack Burkman and Jacob Wohl to secure the pardon, the largest pardon-lobbying disclosure in the Senate database at the time. Trumps own U.S. attorney had just celebrated Schwartz sentencing months earlier.
description_long: Trump pardoned nursing-home operator Joseph Schwartz in November 2025 after he served approximately three months of a three-year sentence. Schwartz had pleaded guilty in a $38 million payroll-tax fraud case. The supplied account says he paid $960,000 to Trump-linked lobbyists Jack Burkman and Jacob Wohl to seek the pardon, describing the disclosure as the largest pardon-lobbying payment in the Senate database at that time. The lobbying payment is a documented route for seeking clemency, not proof that the money was paid to Trump personally or that a criminal exchange occurred. The account also notes that the administration's own U.S. attorney had celebrated the sentencing months earlier. That contrast highlights the different roles of prosecution and presidential clemency in the same case. The event records the conviction, the shortened imprisonment and the lobbying relationship. It does not establish a judicial finding that the pardon was purchased or resolve what happened to every remaining financial obligation.
